title: The Inheritance of Ephraim
summary: The allotment of the descendants of Joseph is described, beginning with the shared southern border that runs from Jericho up through Bethel and down past Beth-horon to Gezer and the sea. Then the borders of Ephraim, Joseph's younger son, are traced in more detail, with a note that some Ephraimite towns lay within Manasseh's land. The chapter ends by noting that Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer but made them forced laborers.
story: After Judah in the south, the book turns to the second great block of territory: the central hill country given to the house of Joseph. Jacob had adopted Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own (Genesis 48:5), so Joseph receives a double portion through two tribes, and Jacob had placed the younger, Ephraim, ahead of the elder (Genesis 48:17-20). This chapter gives Ephraim's land, and chapter 17 gives Manasseh's. Ephraim was Joshua's own tribe (Numbers 13:8), and its territory would hold Shiloh, where the tabernacle is set up in chapter 18. The chapter is short, and it ends on the same kind of sober note as Judah's: a Canaanite city left in place.
historical:
Ephraim's land lay in the central hills north of Jerusalem, well watered and fertile compared with Judah's, with good terraced slopes for olives and vines. Its southern border followed the line from Jericho up to Bethel and down the Beth-horon ridge to Gezer, the route along which the battle of chapter 10 was fought. Bethel, identified with Luz (verse 2; Genesis 28:19), was the place where Jacob dreamed of the ladder, and it later became one of the two royal sanctuaries of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-29).

Gezer, guarding the road from the coast to the hills, was a major city. The Egyptian Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) lists Gezer among places the pharaoh claims to have seized. According to 1 Kings 9:16, a later pharaoh captured Gezer, killed its Canaanites, and gave the city as a dowry to his daughter when she married Solomon, who then rebuilt it. That is the first time the Bible records Gezer fully in Israelite hands. A small limestone tablet found there in 1908, the Gezer Calendar, lists the months of the farming year and is often dated to around the tenth century BC. Over time Ephraim became the leading tribe of the north, so much so that the prophets, especially Hosea, use its name for the whole northern kingdom.
cultural:
Forced labor (mas) meant compulsory work for the state or the dominant group, such as building, farming, or quarrying, usually by conquered peoples. Deuteronomy 20:11 allowed it for distant cities that surrendered, but for the peoples within Canaan the law commanded that they be driven out. Ephraim's arrangement at Gezer is therefore a compromise: the Canaanites were subjected but not removed. Later, Solomon imposed forced labor on the remaining Canaanite peoples (1 Kings 9:20-21) and, controversially, on Israelites as well (1 Kings 5:13), a burden that helped split the kingdom after his death (1 Kings 12:4).

The mention of Ephraimite towns inside Manasseh's territory (verse 9) reflects how real tribal boundaries worked: families settled where they could, and border towns sometimes belonged to one tribe while standing in another's land.
literary: The chapter is a boundary description in two parts. Verses 1-4 trace the southern border of Joseph's combined allotment from east to west and close with a summary: “So Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, received their inheritance.” Verses 5-10 trace Ephraim's own borders, moving from the south to the north and then east, down to Jericho and the Jordan, and west to the Brook of Kanah and the sea. Compared with Judah's chapter it is brief, and unlike Judah's it gives no list of towns. It ends with a formula already heard at the end of chapter 15, “to this day,” pointing to the narrator's own time, when Canaanites still lived at Gezer.

outline.t: The southern border of the house of Joseph
Canaanites left in Gezer as forced laborers

doctrines.note: Ephraim's land fulfills Jacob's blessing, in which the younger son was placed first. As so often in Genesis, God's choice does not follow the expected order of birth, and the allotment carries that choice into the life of the nation.

Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer; it chose to profit from them instead. The choice looks practical, but the book presents it as falling short of the LORD's command, and Judges 2:1-3 warns that such peoples will become thorns in Israel's side.

words.note: Mas, forced labor or a labor gang. It describes people compelled to work for others. Here it marks a compromise: Ephraim subjected the Canaanites of Gezer instead of driving them out. The word returns in the stories of Solomon's building projects and the resentment they caused.

Ephraim. Joseph named his second son with a word that sounds like fruitful, saying that God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction (Genesis 41:52). The tribe's fertile land fits the name, and Ephraim became the leading tribe of the north.

Nachalah, inheritance. The word frames the chapter (verses 5, 8, and 9). It reminds the reader that Ephraim's territory is not something the tribe earned but a share in the land the LORD gave to Jacob's family.

christ: The link is thematic. The story of Ephraim, the younger son placed ahead of the elder, is part of a pattern that runs through Genesis: Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph over his older brothers, Ephraim over Manasseh. The pattern shows that God's blessing comes by his gracious choice, not by natural right or rank. Paul draws on this pattern in Romans 9:10-13 to show that God's purposes stand by his calling rather than by human works. Jesus himself turned expected order upside down, saying that the last will be first and the first last (Matthew 20:16), and the gospel reaches those with no claim to it. The chapter's closing compromise also shows why a better king and a deeper victory would be needed.

hard.q: Was making the Canaanites forced laborers a kindness, a failure, or an injustice?
hard.a: Readers see this verse in more than one light. Within the book's own framework, the point is failure: the LORD had commanded that the peoples of the land be driven out, and Ephraim settled for profitable coexistence, a choice that led to later trouble. From a modern moral standpoint, forced labor is itself troubling, and readers rightly ask how it fits with the law's concern for the stranger and the slave. Some note that the Canaanites of Gezer lived, which was more than the ban allowed, and that the Bible reports this arrangement without praising it. Others point out that later Scripture remembers Solomon's forced labor as a heavy yoke that helped divide the kingdom (1 Kings 12:4). The text is best read as describing what Ephraim did, not as endorsing it, and it invites the reader to see that compromise with a command can produce a second wrong rather than a middle way.

questions: Ephraim chose to profit from what it was told to remove. Where are you tempted to make a practical compromise with something God has asked you to put away?
God placed the younger son first. How does God's habit of choosing the unexpected challenge the way you rank people, including yourself?
Ephraim's land was fertile and strong, and its tribe became powerful and at times proud. How can blessing become a danger if it is not received with gratitude?
